chunks: I2C clock stretching. The question: Explain clock stretching.
Clock stretching is when an I2C target holds the clock wire low to tell the controller "wait, I'm not ready."
It works because the clock wire is shared by all chips, and any chip can pull it low. The wire goes high only when everyone lets go.
The controller must therefore release the clock, then check that it really went high before going on. It suits slow targets but costs speed.
Imagine a teacher dictating a sentence one word at a time to a student who writes. The teacher says each word and moves on at a steady pace.
If the student needs more time, they hold up a hand, and the teacher waits until it goes down. The teacher must look up to see whether the hand is still raised.
The hand is the target pulling the clock low.
The orange row is the target. It begins holding SCL low just after a falling edge (period 2).
The controller (blue) releases SCL at period 3 (dashed means "released"), but the bus row (bottom) stays low until the target releases at period 5: the stretch.
SDA does not change during it. Only at period 5 does the bus clock rise and the controller can continue; its measured high time starts then.
Clock stretching: a target holding the clock wire low to make the controller wait.
Wired-AND clock: the clock wire is low if any chip pulls it low, and high only if all release it ("Advantages of open-drain outputs").
Release and check: the controller lets go of the clock, then reads it back to see whether it is really high.
Timeout: a limit on how long the controller will wait, so a stuck target can't hang everything.
Controller and target: the chip that runs the clock and starts transfers, and the chip that answers.
At 400 kilohertz, one byte takes 9 clock ticks, which is 22. 5 microseconds. Suppose the target stretches the clock 50 microseconds on every byte. Each byte now takes 72.
5 microseconds, so the effective speed is 9 bits per 72. 5 microseconds, about 124 kilohertz. A target that never lets go hangs the bus, so timeouts exist. That is the whole idea.
"Clock stretching is a target holding SCL low to make the controller wait. Because SCL is open-drain, the bus only goes high when both release it.
After releasing SCL, the controller must read it back and wait for it to actually go high before continuing.
It's used by slow targets like MCUs running an ISR or sensors mid-conversion.
The downside is lower throughput and, if a target never lets go, a hung bus, which is why SMBus has a roughly 25 to 35 milliseconds timeout."
